summary.text: The cell membrane is a semipermeable lipid bilayer that separates and protects the interior of a cell from the outside environment.
The bilayer usually consists of phospholipids and glycolipids, and membrane proteins serve as transporters or as enzymes that help the cell interact with its environment.
It controls the movement of substances in and out of a cell and takes part in processes such as cell adhesion and cell signaling.

items.prompt: Gorter and Grendel extracted lipid from mature mammalian red blood cells to study the membrane. Why were those cells a clever choice?

options.label: They have no nuclei or organelles, so the plasma membrane is their only lipid-containing structure
They have the thickest membranes of any cell, which are easiest to measure
They contain no proteins, so their membranes are pure lipid
They are the largest cells, so they give the most lipid to work with

items.explain: Mature mammalian red blood cells lack a nucleus and organelles, so all the extracted lipid could be assumed to come from the plasma membrane.

items.prompt: The extracted lipid covered roughly double the surface area calculated for the cells it came from. What did the researchers conclude about the membrane?

options.label: It has a single layer of lipid with protein on top
It is made mostly of protein, with little lipid
It is thinner than any single molecule could be
It has two layers of lipid, a bilayer

items.explain: The roughly 2:1 area ratio led them to conclude the plasma membrane contains a lipid bilayer.

items.prompt: In the late 1800s scientists argued over whether cell membranes existed at all. What was a main reason?

options.label: Only plant cells had been observed, and plants have no membrane
Membranes dissolve whenever cells are stained for viewing
Microscopes were not yet good enough to tell membranes from cell walls
Everyone agreed membranes were vital, so nobody tested the idea

items.explain: By the second half of the 19th century, microscopy still could not distinguish cell membranes from cell walls, and many refuted the membrane's existence.

items.prompt: A 1930s model pictured the membrane as a lipid bilayer sandwiched between thin layers of another substance. What was that substance?

options.label: Cholesterol
Protein
Cellulose
Water

items.explain: The paucimolecular model suggested a lipid bilayer lay between two thin protein layers.

items.prompt: A cell lets certain ions and organic molecules cross its boundary but keeps others out. Which property of the membrane allows this?

options.label: It is a rigid wall that nothing can cross
It is selectively permeable
It is fully open, so only concentration decides
It is welded shut by peripheral proteins

items.explain: The cell membrane controls what moves in and out and is selectively permeable to ions and organic molecules.

items.prompt: Which molecule, placed between the lipids of an animal cell's membrane, helps keep it suitably fluid across temperatures?

options.label: Glycolipid, which hardens the membrane at every temperature
Cellulose, which gives the membrane a firm frame
Cholesterol, a sterol
Peripheral protein, which melts the lipids apart

items.explain: Eukaryotes typically have sterols such as cholesterol (in animals) between the lipids, maintaining appropriate membrane fluidity at various temperatures.

beats.title: A boundary that chooses
beats.hook: Scientists worked out the structure of the cell's boundary by spreading its fat on water and measuring.

beats.prompt: Researchers extract all the lipid from red blood cells and spread it in one layer on water. If the cell membrane is a double layer of lipid, how will the spread-out area compare with the cells' surface area?
beats.explain: The ratio of the water surface covered to the cells' surface area was approximately 2:1, which led to the bilayer conclusion.

choices.label: About ten times as large
choices.feedback: The measured ratio was far smaller, about 2:1.

choices.label: About half as large
choices.feedback: Spreading lipid out cannot make it cover less than the cells' own surface if it was a bilayer.

choices.label: About the same
choices.feedback: That would fit a single layer, but the membrane has two layers, so the lipid covers more.

paragraphs.heading: The cell's border
paragraphs.text: The cell membrane, also called the plasma membrane, is the boundary around a cell. It keeps the inside of the cell apart from the space outside and shields it. It is semipermeable: it lets some things through and keeps others out, deciding which ions and organic molecules get in or out.

paragraphs.heading: What it is made of
paragraphs.text: Its base is a lipid bilayer, usually built from phospholipids and glycolipids. Many cells also tuck sterols, such as cholesterol in animals, between these lipids, and the sterols keep the membrane suitably fluid at different temperatures. Proteins are set into it too. Integral proteins cross the whole membrane and act as transporters, while peripheral proteins sit on its surface and work as enzymes that help the cell deal with its surroundings. Glycolipids in the outer layer play a similar part.

paragraphs.heading: Other jobs
paragraphs.text: The membrane does more than guard the door. It takes part in cell adhesion, in ion conductivity and in cell signaling. It also gives other structures something to hold on to: the cell wall and a carbohydrate coat called the glycocalyx on the outside, and the cytoskeleton, a network of protein fibers on the inside. In synthetic biology, scientists can even put cell membranes back together artificially.

paragraphs.heading: A long-ignored structure
paragraphs.text: For a long time the membrane went unnoticed. After Robert Hooke discovered cells in 1665, people at first thought all cells had a hard wall, since only plant cells could be observed then. Microscopists studied the cell wall for more than 150 years. Even in the later 1800s, microscopes could not tell a membrane from a wall, though some workers reasoned that animal cells must have one, because parts moved around inside the cell but not outside it. Many still doubted it near the end of that century, and an 1890 revision of the cell theory treated membranes as merely secondary.

paragraphs.heading: Made of lipids
paragraphs.text: Studies of osmosis and permeability finally brought the membrane more attention. In 1895 Ernest Overton proposed that it was built from lipids. In 1925 Gorter and Grendel took the lipid out of human red blood cells and spread it over water to see how much surface it covered. Mature mammalian red blood cells have no nucleus or organelles, so all their lipid comes from the membrane. The lipid covered about twice the area of the cells' surface, so they concluded the membrane holds a lipid bilayer.

paragraphs.heading: Changing models
paragraphs.text: In the 1930s most scientists came to accept the model of Davson and Danielli, from 1935, which placed a lipid bilayer between two thin layers of protein. It led the field for about 30 years. Then in 1972 Singer and Nicolson put forward the fluid mosaic model. Long after the 1970s, it is still the main picture of the cell membrane.

paragraphs.heading: Many names
paragraphs.text: The structure has gone by many names, including plasma membrane, cytoplasmic membrane, cell envelope and Plasmahaut, meaning plasma skin. The term plasmalemma was coined by Mast in 1924. Some authors who doubted that the cell had a working permeable boundary at its surface preferred that word for the cell's outer region.
